kp.k: Professional judgment remains subject to objective reasonable care
kp.d: The Supreme Court of Georgia holds that an attorney's honest exercise of professional judgment does not alone defeat a malpractice claim: courts must examine whether the attorney exercised reasonable care in reaching that judgment. This is a holding about professional negligence, not a finding about AI use, which the opinion does not address.
qs: And in doing so, Hudson supplanted the long-standing analysis centered on the objective standard of reasonable care with a subjective analysis focused on whether a particular defendant engaged in an “honest exercise” of professional judgment and, as such, was entitled to judgmental immunity.

Accordingly, in determining whether Cox-Ott had established the requisite element of her malpractice claim, the Court of Appeals erred by considering only whether Leonard “engaged in an honest exercise of professional judgment,” but instead should have determined, under the circumstances of this case, whether Leonard exercised reasonable care in reaching that judgment.

kp.k: Experience alone does not establish reasonable care
kp.d: The Court rejects the lower court's reliance on Leonard's litigation experience as sufficient protection for his recommendation to proceed under Georgia rather than New York law. Its ruling requires a circumstances-specific reasonable-care inquiry; it does not itself find that Leonard was negligent or prescribe a categorical research requirement.
qs: But the mere fact that an attorney's judgment is based on his experience does not automatically establish that the attorney exercised reasonable care in reaching that judgment such that he should be insulated from liability.

In particular, the Court of Appeals held that research into the choice of law issue was not required in order for Leonard's decision to be protected by judgmental immunity and that Leonard's recommendation as to venue was similarly protected because of his expertise and experience.

kp.k: Mistaken judgments do not necessarily constitute malpractice
kp.d: Drawing on Georgia precedent and English common law, the Court preserves attorneys' discretion in matters of professional judgment while conditioning that discretion on reasonable care. The standard requires neither extraordinary diligence nor guaranteed success; whether skill and diligence were adequate depends on the particular facts and circumstances.

Good faith must exist on the part of the attorney towards his client, and when this is shown, the absence or presence of reasonable skill and diligence must in each case be determined by its own facts.

kp.k: Judgmental immunity is not a separate liability shield
kp.d: The Court overrules Hudson v. Windholz (1992) and decisions relying on it only to the extent that they omit the reasonable-care standard. It also recommends discarding the judgmental-immunity label because the underlying question concerns breach of the standard of care, rather than an immunity for professional decisions.
qs: to the extent they omit consideration of the reasonable care standard when analyzing a legal malpractice claim.
We note that the moniker “judgmental-immunity doctrine” is a misnomer that should be discarded.

As courts in other jurisdictions have recognized, the judgmental-immunity “doctrine” does not, in fact, grant immunity to attorneys for actions or omissions based on the exercise of professional judgment.

kp.k: Malpractice requires a task-linked breach and causation
kp.d: The Court describes malpractice as professional negligence arising from the attorney-client relationship. The plaintiff must establish employment, failure to exercise ordinary care, skill and diligence, and proximate causation of damage. Breach must concern the task for which the attorney was employed, while causation requires showing that the plaintiff would have prevailed in the underlying case but for the negligence.
qs: “(1) employment of the defendant attorney, (2) failure of the attorney to exercise ordinary care, skill[,] and diligence, and (3) that such negligence was the proximate cause of damage to the plaintiff.”

“It is axiomatic that the element of breach of duty in a legal malpractice case — the failure to exercise ordinary care, skill, and diligence — must relate directly to the duty of the attorney, that is, the duty to perform the task for which he was employed.”
“And in order to establish the final element, the plaintiff must show that, but for the attorney's negligence in the underlying case, the plaintiff would have prevailed.”

kp.k: Failure of causation independently sustains judgment for attorneys
kp.d: Despite rejecting the judgmental-immunity reasoning, the Supreme Court affirms judgment for Leonard and Barnes & Thornburg because the Court of Appeals' separate determination that Cox-Ott failed to establish causation remained undisturbed. The outcome therefore does not establish that Leonard satisfied the corrected standard of care; it demonstrates that breach and causation are distinct requirements.
qs: Besides concluding that Cox-Ott's claims were barred by judgmental immunity, the Court of Appeals also held that Cox-Ott failed to establish the causation element of her professional malpractice claim.
As a result, the judgment of the Court of Appeals must be affirmed on that basis.
